new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible primary descriptions (Santandrea 1963, 1964) treat Kare as a tone language with three levels (high, low, mid) and mark tone only sporadically; neither says anything about word stress or accent placement. No stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the 1964 note adds that some 3rd-person possessive forms 'differ only in tone' and that one tonal observation is 'a rather poor foundation to build any theory upon' (Santandrea 1964: ca. 105-106).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone marking on wordlist citation forms (Kare A and Kare B varieties of the South Sudan remnant groups). Nothing on stress at word or phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea's 'Kare' is the remnant Kare population of Western Bahr el Ghazal (South Sudan), which he splits into 'Kare A' and 'Kare B' varieties (Kare B has mj where Kare A has nz, etc.); Glottolog links both Santandrea articles to kari1306, the Congolese Bantu Kari/Kare (Guthrie D.301) also recorded by Dijkmans 1927-1947 as the 'restvolk Kare'. Glottolog 5.3 classifies it as Bantu (Ngombe-Ababuan > Ababuan > Old Bomokandian > Ngbele-Ngenda), not Ubangian. The Glottolog-linked Enfield 2005 sketch is a different language (Kri/Kàrì, Vietic, Laos).
